Chapter 3: The Crown of Thorns and the Cost of Love.
When you think of a crown, what comes to mind? Probably power, honor, maybe even celebration. But the crown that was pressed onto Jesus’s head was nothing like that. It was made of thorns—sharp, twisted, and designed to hurt. The soldiers weren’t just mocking him; they were turning the idea of a crown upside down, using it to wound and to ridicule.
But here’s the thing—there’s a message underneath all that pain and cruelty. Imagine someone you know, or maybe even yourself, feeling misunderstood or ridiculed. Maybe you’ve put in your best effort, only to be met with scorn. That’s what the crown of thorns represents: love that’s willing to be misunderstood, to carry the weight of rejection, and even endure humiliation. This wasn’t just about physical pain, either. It cut deep, right to the heart of dignity and self-worth.
Those thorns digging into the skin, drawing blood—they became a symbol of just how broken our world can be. Every harsh word, every act of cruelty, every moment of shame—somehow, all of that was woven into that crown. And yet, Jesus wore it willingly. Not because he was defeated, but as if to say, “Love isn’t going to be stopped by pain or by mockery.”
So, why does this matter for us? Think about how often the fear of rejection hangs over people’s lives. The longing to belong, to be accepted, can sometimes lead us to hide who we really are or to settle for less. But the crown of thorns flips that idea on its head. It shows us that true acceptance doesn’t come from chasing approval, but from a love that’s willing to suffer for the sake of someone else. The price was high, but it was paid—completely.
There’s a quiet strength in enduring suffering for others. The crown of thorns was meant to bring shame, but it actually became a symbol of a love that just won’t give up. If you’ve ever felt rejected or weighed down by shame, know this: you’re not alone. That pain has been understood. Those wounds are shared. And through it all, the love at the center remains unbroken.
